summary: Extends RSVP so it can reserve resources for individual traffic flows protected by IPsec, using the Authentication Header or the Encapsulating Security Payload. Since encrypted packets hide details routers normally use, the extension supplies another way to identify the flow.

plainLanguage.summary:
RSVP is a protocol that asks the network to reserve bandwidth for a particular stream of traffic. To do that it has to say which stream it means, and it normally does that with the destination port number in the transport header.

Encrypted traffic hides that port. RFC 2207 gives RSVP something else to work with: the four-byte number that identifies the encryption session. It also invents a virtual destination port, a number that exists only in the reservation messages, so that several encrypted conversations to the same address can be told apart.

questions: how does rsvp work with ipsec
how to reserve bandwidth for encrypted flows
what is a generalized port identifier
why does rsvp need the spi for ipsec
what is a virtual destination port
subtitle: Teaching RSVP to reserve resources for individual encrypted flows, not just per address.

tldr.problem: RSVP reserves network resources by describing a flow with a destination address, a protocol and a destination port. The IPsec security headers carry no port, so an encrypted flow could only be reserved per address and per protocol, with no way to separate one sender's traffic from another's.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2207 lets RSVP use the IPsec Security Parameter Index where it would normally use a port, carrying it in a new four-byte field called the Generalized Port Identifier. A virtual destination port in a new session object tells apart several sessions that share one destination address.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from September 1997 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It costs nothing per data packet and needs no change to the IPsec headers, but it does not use the IPv6 Flow Label field and offers only limited service with wildcard reservations.

today: RFC 2207 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the RSVP extensions for IPsec flows. The document notes that the approach does not use the IPv6 Flow Label field and leaves that for later work.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Recently published Standards Track RFCs specify protocol mechanisms to provide IP level security. These IP Security, or IPSEC, protocols support packet level authentication and integrity and confidentiality. A number of interoperable implementations already exist and several vendors have announced commercial products that use these mechanisms.

The IPSEC protocols provide service by adding a new header between a packet's IP header and the transport, for example UDP, protocol header. The two security headers are the Authentication Header, for authentication, and the Encapsulating Security Payload, for integrity and confidentiality.

RSVP is being developed as a resource reservation, or dynamic QoS setup, protocol. RSVP as currently specified in RFC 2205 is tailored towards IP packets carrying protocols that have TCP or UDP-like ports. Protocols that do not have such ports, such as the IPSEC protocols, can be supported, but only with limitations. Specifically, for flows of IPSEC data packets, flow definition can only be done on a per IP address, per protocol basis.

This memo proposes extensions to RSVP so that data flows containing IPSEC protocols can be controlled at a granularity similar to what is already specified for UDP and TCP. The extensions can be used with both IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec puts a security header between the IP header and the transport header. The transport header, which holds the port number, is either encrypted or hidden, so RSVP cannot see it.

sections.title: Overview of Extensions
sections.content:
The basic notion is to extend RSVP to use the IPSEC Security Parameter Index, or SPI, in place of the UDP and TCP-like ports. This requires a new FILTER_SPEC object, which contains the IPSEC SPI, and a new SESSION object.

While SPIs are allocated based on destination address, they will typically be associated with a particular sender. Two senders to the same unicast destination will therefore usually have different SPIs. To support the control of multiple independent flows between source and destination IP addresses, the SPI is included as part of the FILTER_SPEC. When using WF, however, all flows to the same IP destination address using the same IP protocol ID share the same reservation. This limitation exists because the IPSEC transport headers do not contain a destination demultiplexing value like the UDP or TCP destination port.

Although the RESV message format does not change, RESV processing requires modification. Processing of the new IPSEC FILTER_SPEC depends on the use of the new SESSION object and on the protocol ID contained in the session definition. When the new FILTER_SPEC object is used, the complete four bytes of the SPI have to be extracted from the FILTER_SPEC for use by the packet classifier. The location of the SPI in the transport header of the IPSEC packets is dependent on the protocol ID field.

The extension also requires a change to PATH processing, specifically in the usage of the port field in a session definition. An RSVP session is defined by the triple of destination address, protocol ID and destination port. The SESSION object defined in RFC 2205 contains UDP or TCP destination ports, specifically a 16-bit quantity carried at the octet offset +2 in the transport header, or zero for protocols that lack such a field. The IPSEC protocols do not contain such a field, but there remains a requirement for demultiplexing sessions beyond the IP destination address. To satisfy it, a virtual destination port, or vDstPort, is introduced. The vDstPort value is carried in the new SESSION object but not in the IPSEC transport header. It allows the differentiation of multiple IPSEC sessions destined to the same IP address.

In PATH messages, the SENDER_TEMPLATE for IPSEC flows has the same format as the modified FILTER_SPEC, but a new SESSION object is used to unambiguously distinguish the use of a virtual destination port. Traffic is mapped to reservations based on the SPIs in FILTER_SPECs. When WF is used, all flows to the same IP destination address and with the same IP protocol ID share the same reservation.

The advantages of the approach are that no changes to RFC 1826 and RFC 1827 are required and that there is no additional per data packet overhead. It does not take advantage of the IPv6 Flow Label field, so greater efficiency may be possible for IPv6 flows; the details of IPv6 Flow Label usage are left for the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new numbers do the work. The Security Parameter Index identifies the encryption session, and it is used in place of a port. The virtual destination port is a number carried only in the reservation messages, so several reservations to the same address can be told apart.

sections.title: Object Definition
sections.content:
The FILTER_SPEC and SENDER_TEMPLATE used with IPSEC protocols contain a four byte field used to carry the SPI. Rather than label the modified field with an IPSEC specific label, the label Generalized Port Identifier, or GPI, is used, so that these objects may be reused for non-IPSEC uses in the future. The names for these objects are the IPv4/GPI FILTER_SPEC, IPv6/GPI FILTER_SPEC, IPv4/GPI SENDER_TEMPLATE and IPv6/GPI SENDER_TEMPLATE. The new SESSION objects are the IPv4/GPI SESSION and the IPv6/GPI SESSION. When referring to the new objects, the IP version is not included unless a specific distinction between IPv4 and IPv6 is being made.

The SESSION class is 1. The IPv4/GPI SESSION object has Class 1 and C-Type 3, and holds the IPv4 destination address in four bytes, then the protocol ID, the flags and the vDstPort. The IPv6/GPI SESSION object has Class 1 and C-Type 4, and holds the IPv6 destination address in sixteen bytes, then the protocol ID, the flags and the vDstPort.

The FILTER_SPEC class is 10. The IPv4/GPI FILTER_SPEC object has Class 10 and C-Type 4, and holds the IPv4 source address in four bytes, then the Generalized Port Identifier. The IPv6/GPI FILTER_SPEC object has Class 10 and C-Type 5, and holds the IPv6 source address in sixteen bytes, then the Generalized Port Identifier.

The SENDER_TEMPLATE class is 11. The IPv4/GPI SENDER_TEMPLATE object has Class 11 and C-Type 4, and the IPv6/GPI SENDER_TEMPLATE object has Class 11 and C-Type 5. Their definitions are the same as the corresponding FILTER_SPEC objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new object shapes are defined, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6 in each case. The session object adds the virtual destination port to the address and protocol. The filter and sender template objects add the four-byte identifier to the source address.

sections.title: Required Processing Changes
sections.content:
The section presents additions to the processing rules presented in RFC 2209, required in order to properly process the GPI SESSION and FILTER_SPEC objects. Values for referenced error codes can be found in RFC 2205. As with the other RSVP documents, values for internally reported API errors are not defined.

Both RESV and PATH processing need to be changed. The PATH message processing changes are these. When a session is defined using the GPI SESSION object, only the GPI SENDER_TEMPLATE may be used; when this condition is violated, end-stations should report a Conflicting C-Type API error to the application. For PATH messages that contain the GPI SESSION object, end-stations must verify that the protocol ID corresponds to a protocol known to use the GPI SESSION object; the values 51 for AH and 50 for ESP must be supported by implementations supporting these IPSEC extensions, and if an unknown protocol ID is used the API should report an API Error. For such messages, the vDstPort value should be recorded; it forms part of the recorded state and is used to match Resv messages, but it is not passed to traffic control, and non-zero values are required, which ensures that a non-GPI SESSION object never merges with a GPI SESSION object. A violation causes an Invalid Destination Port API error.

The changes to RESV message processing are these. When a RESV message contains a GPI FILTER_SPEC, the session must be defined using the GPI SESSION object, otherwise this is a message formatting error. The GPI contained in the FILTER_SPEC must match the GPI contained in the SENDER_TEMPLATE, otherwise a No sender information for this Resv message error is generated. When the GPI FILTER_SPEC is used, each node must create a data classifier for the flow described by the quadruple of destination address, protocol ID, source address and GPI. The data classifier has to look for the four byte GPI at transport header offset +4 for AH and at transport header offset +0 for ESP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node that carries a reservation has to classify incoming packets into the right flow. For an encrypted flow it looks in a different place depending on the protocol: four bytes further in for the Authentication Header, at the start for ESP.

sections.title: Merging Flowspecs and Reservation Styles
sections.content:
When using this extension for IPSEC data flows, RSVP sessions are defined by the triple of destination address, protocol ID and vDstPort. Similarly, a sender is defined by the tuple of source address and GPI, where the GPI field is a four byte representation of a generalized source port. These extensions have some ramifications depending on the reservation style.

In the FF and SE styles, the FILTER_SPEC object contains the source address and GPI pair. This allows the receiver to uniquely identify senders based on both elements of the pair. When merging explicit sender descriptors, the senders may only be considered identical when both elements are identical.

These extensions provide very limited service when used with WF style reservations. As described, the SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC each contain the GPI. In a WF style reservation, the RESV message does not contain a FILTER_SPEC, because it is a wildcard filter, and the SENDER_TEMPLATE is ignored, because any sender is allowed. As a result, classifiers may match all packets which contain both the session's destination IP address and protocol ID to such WF reservations. Although a solution for this limitation is not proposed, the issue is not seen as significant since IPSEC applications are less likely to use WF style reservations.
sections.plainLanguage: With a wildcard reservation, any sender is allowed and the filter is ignored, so the encrypted flow identifier never gets used. The document accepts that limit, on the grounds that IPsec applications rarely ask for wildcard reservations.

sections.title: The vDstPort Ranges
sections.content:
The range of possible vDstPort values is broken down into sections, in a fashion similar to the UDP and TCP port ranges. The value 0 is an illegal value. The range 1 to 10 is reserved, and the authors are to be contacted. The range 11 to 8191 is assigned by IANA. The range 8192 to 65535 is dynamic.

IANA is directed to assign the well-known vDstPorts using the following criteria: anyone who asks for an assigned vDstPort must provide a point of contact, a brief description of intended use, and a short name to be associated with the assignment.
sections.plainLanguage: The virtual destination port numbers are handed out in bands, much like port numbers for TCP and UDP. Zero is not allowed, low numbers are assigned by IANA, and the high band is for dynamic use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same considerations stated in RFC 2205, RFC 1826 and RFC 1827 apply to the extensions described here. There are two additional issues.

First, the vDstPort mechanism represents another data element about the IP flow that might be available to an adversary. Such data might be useful to an adversary engaging in traffic analysis by monitoring not only the data packets of the IP flow but also the RSVP control messages associated with that flow. Protection against traffic analysis attacks is outside the scope of this mechanism. One possible approach to precluding such attacks would be the deployment and use of appropriate link-layer confidentiality mechanisms, such as encryption.

Second, changes in SPI values for a given flow will affect RSVP flows and reservations. Changes happen whenever that flow changes its security association, which occurs when a flow is rekeyed, that is, when it starts to use a new key. Rekeying intervals are typically set based on traffic levels, key size, threat environment and the crypto algorithm in use. When an SPI change occurs it will, in most cases, be necessary to send the corresponding SENDER_TEMPLATEs and FILTER_SPECs. IPSEC implementations, RSVP applications and RSVP end-station implementations will need to take the possibility of changes of SPI into account to ensure proper reservation behaviour.

Many, if not most, RSVP sessions will not need to deal with this rekeying issue. For those that do, the impact of sending new PATH and RESV messages varies based on the reservation style being used. The least impact of an SPI change is on WF style reservations, where a new SENDER_TEMPLATE has to be sent but no new RESV is required. For SE style reservations, both a new SENDER_TEMPLATE and a new RESV have to be sent, which results in changes to state but should not affect data packet delivery or actual resource allocation in any way. The FF style is impacted the most: like SE, both PATH and RESV messages have to be sent, and since FF style reservations result in the sender receiving its own resource allocation, resources will be allocated twice for a period of time, or there will not be enough resources to support the new flow without first freeing the old one.

A way around the FF problem does exist. Applications that want FF style reservations can use multiple SE reservations, with each real sender having a separate SESSION and vDstPort definition. When it came time to switch SPIs, a shared reservation could be made for the new SPI while the old SPI was still active, and once the new SPI was in use the old reservation could be torn down. This is less than optimal, but provides uninterrupted service for a set of applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Two risks come with the extension. The virtual destination port is another visible clue about a flow, which can help an attacker watching the network. And when the encryption key is changed, the flow's identifier changes with it, so the reservation has to be updated.

sections.title: Options Considered
sections.content:
The appendix reviews other approaches that were explored in developing the extensions, to provide additional context into the general problem. All listed options were rejected by the working group.

UDP encapsulation would add a UDP header between the IP and the IPSEC AH or ESP headers. Since the current SESSION and FILTER objects expect UDP or TCP ports, the proposal was to give it to them. The advantage is that no RSVP changes are required. The disadvantage is that, since the headers are not in the expected location, RFC 1826 and RFC 1827 are violated.

FlowID Header encapsulation would add a new type of header between the IP and the IPSEC AH or ESP headers, with source port, destination port, version, length, protocol ID and checksum. It separates flow identification from all other protocol processing, but adding a header violates RFC 1826 and RFC 1827, and applications using RSVP have to add the extra header on all data packets whose transport headers lack UDP or TCP like ports.

IPSEC protocol modification would leave RSVP as currently specified and use the Security Association Identifier found in the IPSEC headers for flow identification. The SPI is in the wrong location when using AH, since UDP and TCP have port assignments in the first four bytes of their headers while the ESP header has the SPI in the same location and AH does not. The SPI is also normally selected by the receiver and is likely to be different for each sender, and selecting it before starting the RSVP session extends setup time by at least one round trip time.

AH transparency would skip over the Authentication Header in packet classifier processing. With ESP packets the real source and destination ports are encrypted and therefore useless to RSVP, but for AH the real header follows the Authentication Header, so it would be possible to use the transport header for RSVP session definition. The major disadvantage is that routers and hosts must skip all AHs before classifying packets, and the working group decided that it was best to have a consistent solution for both AH and ESP.
sections.plainLanguage: Four other approaches were considered and rejected. Two of them would have added a header to every data packet, and two of them would have changed the IPsec specifications or made routers do extra work.

fields.name: Generalized Port Identifier
fields.desc: Four bytes carrying the IPsec Security Parameter Index, used in place of a transport port.

fields.name: IPv4 DestAddress
fields.desc: The destination address of the session.

fields.name: Protocol ID
fields.desc: The IP protocol ID. Implementations supporting these extensions must support 51 for AH and 50 for ESP.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: The flags field of the session object.

fields.name: vDstPort
fields.desc: The virtual destination port. It is carried in the session object and not in the IPsec transport header.

viz.caption: The four approaches the working group rejected

items.title: UDP encapsulation
items.text: Add a UDP header between the IP and the IPsec headers, so RSVP can use ordinary ports. It would violate the IPsec header specifications.

items.title: FlowID header encapsulation
items.text: Add a new header carrying ports, a protocol ID and a checksum. It separates flow identification from other processing, but every data packet gains a header.

items.title: IPsec protocol modification
items.text: Use the SPI directly in RSVP. The SPI sits in the wrong place for AH, and it is chosen by the receiver, which forces the sender to wait a round trip before starting.

items.title: AH transparency
items.text: Skip over the Authentication Header when classifying packets. It would work for AH but not ESP, and it makes routers and hosts do extra work.
